Posted February 5, 2003
Analysis by Richard Cowan

The Gateway theory, hypothesis, effect, is the name given to the statistical fact that most users of hard drugs had previously used cannabis. The inference of causality is the logical error which text books call post hoc ergo propter hoc. After this therefore because of this.

Moreover, I think the assumption that there is such a thing as a gateway drug is the error of hypostatization, treating an abstract concept as though it were something real.

Is the first drug used a gateway, stepping stone, threshold, etc., to whatever drugs are subsequently used?

No one would ever use drugs, if they did not start using drugs. If there is a second drug, there will always be a first drug, but is it a gateway. "? The debate over the gateway is simply a debate over the meaning of an established statistical fact.

There is a cliché scene at the end of horror movies in which the monster, seemingly dead and buried, suddenly thrusts its hand up from its freshly dug grave. The gateway theory seems to have similar problems staying dead.

Just when you thought it was safe to go back into the public discourse, it's alive!

In late January, while MarijuanaNews was changing servers, JAMA, the Journal of the American Medical Association, published an article Escalation of Drug Use in Early-Onset Cannabis Users vs Co-twin Controls.

It was a study of identical twins in Australia by Michael T. Lynskey of the Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis. It resurrected the gateway again.

Actually, I was rather glad that I had to wait to write about it, because it was really hard to figure out what to say about it again, until the prohibitionist media did their usual sloppy work.

In December, The RAND Corp. published a statistical analysis of the data that has been used to support the gateway effect. It seemed to bury the monster again.
See
 Famous Think Tank Discovers That the Gateway Is A Fraud, But Everything Else That the Prohibitionists Tell Us Is Still True. They Have An Office In Holland But Ignore the Dutch Experience.
and links

According to Andrew Morral, associate director of RAND's Public Safety and Justice unit and lead author of the study, " We've shown that the marijuana gateway effect is not the best explanation for the link between marijuana use and the use of harder drugs. An alternative, simpler and more compelling explanation accounts for the pattern of drug use you see in this country, without resort to any gateway effects. While the gateway theory has enjoyed popular acceptance, scientists have always had their doubts. Our study shows that these doubts are justified. "

The RAND study received quite a bit of publicity, but since prohibition causes short and long term memory loss, it was ignored less than two months later when the JAMA report came out.

For example, HealthScoutNews reported, Marijuana really is a gateway drug that leads to use of harder drugs, new research contends.

HealthScoutNews made no mention of the RAND study. But then, the author of the HealthScoutNews article does not seem to have actually read the JAMA report either. In fact, the most interesting thing about the comments on the JAMA article was that almost no one who wrote about seems to have actually read it.

Well, the editors of the New Scientist did.

Their article, Marijuana's link to hard drug use not genetic, said, Nonetheless, the research shows that the gateway is real, so what implications does this have for drug laws?

" This finding can be used as the bases for quite opposite drug policies, " Lynskey told New Scientist.

The problem is that researchers are no nearer understanding the mechanism of the gateway. If taking cannabis causes physiological effects in the brain that predispose the smoker to other drugs, then the message for lawmakers is that keeping people away from cannabis will also keep them off heroin and cocaine.

On the other hand, if cannabis smokers move on to harder drugs simply because they have access to them through drug dealers, then decriminalisation ought to reduce hard drug use. (emphasis added)
 (MarijuanaNews note: Actually, it would take legalization to do that.)
See
 Vraag Een Politieagent. Go Ahead, Ask A Cop For Dope. The Dutch Don't Mind New Scientist Special Report

Please note: the author of the study acknowledged that keeping cannabis in the same markets as hard drugs could be the gateway.

Somehow that did not make it to the popular media. Why?

Well, guess who paid for the accompanying JAMA editorial Does Marijuana Use Cause the Use of Other Drugs?by Denise B. Kandel, PhD, Department of Psychiatry, Columbia University? That's right, Work on this editorial was supported by Research Scientist Award DA00081 from the National Institute on Drug Abuse.

NIDA, the scientific arm of the DEAland prohibitionist propaganda machine, pays for 85% of the so-called research on drug abuse in the world. They don't try to buy the scientists, they just buy the spin.
See
 As Predicted, NIDA Buys Its Press Release: " Marijuana has as much potential for abuse  as cocaine and heroin. "

And Kandel delivered. Consider this scientific gem from her editorial: will preventing the use of marijuana prevent the use of other illicit drugs?

Hopefully it will, for prevention efforts will presumably affect the underlying risk and protective factors related to the onset of marijuana use, whether or not these factors are shared with the onset of the use of other illicit drugs. (emphasis added)

Hopefully??? Now that's hard science!
See
What If Marijuana Disappeared? By Richard Cowan

Now contrast that with Lynskey's speculation, if cannabis smokers move on to harder drugs simply because they have access to them through drug dealers, then decriminalisation ought to reduce hard drug use.

However, there is another environmental factor that might explain why the twin who used cannabis at an early age might be more likely to use hard drugs than his non-toking wombmate.

The cannabis-using twin will have found out that they were being lied to about cannabis and might then make the common error of assuming that they had been lied to about everything else.

Cannabis prohibition creates the gateway between cannabis and hard drugs by keeping them in the same distribution channels and then undermines the credibility of drug education by lying about cannabis. This is the premise for all of The Netherlands drugs policies. The Dutch have a much lower rate of both cannabis and hard drug use than does DEAland and Australia.

Will NIDA pay for an editorial reporting that?

Until it is recognized that cannabis prohibition is not just a failure, but a counterproductive fraud that creates the evil that it claims to fight, the gateway theory will keep coming back like the fictional monster that it really is.
